title: Eclipse
subtitle: A Billion Small Flames
dedication: For anyone who was told there wasn’t enough light to go around.

epigraph.text: Salvation that requires a famine is not salvation. It is administration.
epigraph.attribution: Ren Kael, later, to no one in particular

chapters.title: The Warm Cell
paragraphs: The latch on the inner door stuck, as it always stuck, and Cardinal Solenne put her shoulder to it without calling for a novice. Heat spilled over her knuckles. The Warm Cell was a square of dressed basalt no wider than a confession stall, lit by a brazier the size of a begging bowl, and it had been her true office since the night she laid Halvern under glass. She did not sit. She never sat when the work was waiting. She took the iron spiral in the floor and went down into the Vault of Cinders with one hand on the rail, counting the turns the way other women counted beads.

The vault received her the way a held breath receives a name. Six coffins stood in a ring around a shallow dish of cinder-glass, each coffin the length of a grown body and the color of a quenched forge, each bound with seals that had once been bright as well-shards and were now the dull red of old scabs. The air down here was not the thin rationed warmth of Cindrel's streets. It was a stored heat, a hoarded heat, the leftover fever of six people who had tried to be the sun and had been put to bed for it. Solenne walked the ring as she always walked it, clockwise, and she spoke the names because unnamed things learned how to get up.

Vael first. The Kiln. The coffin was pitted along one side where his heat had tried to eat the iron from within, four hundred years ago, before the Church had understood that a vessel could starve a city by shining. She set two fingers on the lid and felt the slow pull of him, the old hunger that had never learned to be a hearth. Torren next, the captain who had warmed an army until the army cooked in its own armor; his seals were military knots, ugly and sure. Iven after that, who had written that the Hollow Sun was a door and not a corpse, and who had opened himself to prove it. Iven's glass was the clearest. She could see the outline of a man with his hands folded, and if she was not careful she could mistake the pose for peace.

Halvern's coffin stood at the fourth mark, and she stopped there longer than the rite required. The glass over him had been poured in a single night with her own calorancy in the mix, and it had never clouded. He looked as he had looked at twenty-nine, which was a cruelty she had chosen and would choose again. Dark hair. A mouth that had argued with her in kitchens and in choir lofts and once, disastrously, in the well-court in front of the old Cardinal. She had loved that mouth. She had put a seal over it anyway. *Managed dusk*, she had told him, when he still had a voice to call her a coward. *A noon that belongs to one body will eat the rest.* He had not believed her. The Hollow Sun had twitched in its socket the night he peaked, the same way it had twitched for the boy in Vireth, and she had done the only work left to a person who loved the world more than one man. "I kept the cell," she said, which was not a prayer. "It is still too warm. You would complain."

Sera's coffin was smaller. That was the fact of it, and Solenne did not decorate the fact. Twelve years old, wrists like kindling, a well-brat from the ash-lanes who had lit a whole district by accident and then asked, politely, if she could light the rest. Inquisitor Voss had held the child still while the seals went on. Voss had been twenty and certain. Solenne had been certain too. Certainty was a tool. She used it until it broke, and then she had it reforged. The glass over Sera showed a girl with her eyes closed and a smear of gold still caught in the lashes, as if noon had tried to leave a forwarding address.

The sixth had no name because names were how vessels taught the living to miss them. He had been a slum boy from the canal-side of Cindrel, fourteen or fifteen, caught in the first hour of his waking with a three-legged mutt barking itself hoarse at his heels. He looked enough like the Vireth boy that Solenne had, for one unprofessional breath, wondered if the god recycled faces. She had sealed him before he learned a technique worth copying. His coffin hummed at a pitch the others did not, a thin, unfinished note. She had always disliked that note. It sounded like a sentence that had been cut off in a kitchen.

The dish at the center of the ring was new work. She had spent the last year on it, in the hours when the court wanted hymns and Cassian Vale wanted to be told he was a sun. The dish was reverse-calorancy: six channels of seal-iron inlaid in a pattern Iven had once sketched in a margin and then crossed out, because Iven had still believed in doors. The pattern did not open. It drank. If the six were chained through it, their stored noon would pull inward instead of spilling, a snuffing well, a throat for heat. A weapon against a seventh. She had not told the novices what it was. She had told them it was a reliquary. In her experience the two were often the same object. She crouched and checked the inlay with a thumbnail. One channel had hairline frost in it, which was wrong. Frost did not belong in the Vault of Cinders. Frost belonged to the woman in the Nightlands who called herself a mother and marched like a season. Solenne scraped the frost out with the edge of a seal-key and watched it die on her skin as a single bead of water. *Not yet*, she thought, and was not sure whether she meant the frost or the weapon.

A sound came down the spiral: boots, then the particular cough of a man who had been told not to run in holy places and had run anyway. Brother Kest appeared on the last turn with his cap in his hands and ice in his eyebrows. He was young enough to still believe that ice on a messenger was a kind of proof. "Eminence," he said, and then, because she did not fill silences for other people, he filled this one himself. "The north gate sent a flare. Frost-line is inside the outer farms. And the cistern watch reports heat that is not on the tithe-books. Gold heat. Moving."

Solenne stood. Her knees did not crack. She had spent too much stored warmth on the small vanities of a body that still had work to do. "Cassian?" Kest's mouth did something unhappy. "In his apartments, Eminence. He asked not to be called unless the disk moved. He has not worn the saint-harness since the boy beat him without killing him. The shard in his chest is quiet. The hymn-keys are still in his keeping." She did not raise her voice. Kest leaned in to hear her, which was the old trick, and she watched him understand that he had been given an order dressed as a forecast. "They will not be by evening. Go back up. Seal the well-court. No one in or out of the Spire but Church. If Mother Ash wants a conversation, she may have it with the walls."

Kest hesitated. The hesitation was the most honest thing he had brought down the stairs. "The gold heat, Eminence. The watch thinks it is him. The Vireth boy. In the cisterns. Inside the city." Solenne said, "I know what they think." She knew because the sixth coffin had changed its note while Kest was still talking. The unfinished hum had found a harmony. It was a small sound, smaller than a kettle, and it made the hair along her arms lift as if a door had opened in a house she had locked herself. The other five lids did not move. Halvern did not move. But the ring as a whole had the attention of a room that had been waiting for a seventh chair.

Solenne crossed to the nameless coffin and laid her palm on the glass. The boy inside did not wake. He was not allowed to. What woke was the leftover calor in him, the scrap of god-heat that recognized its own kin walking the pipes above their heads. Ren Kael. Street rat. Primordial Calor with a dog and a pair of borrowed adults. The dream becoming lucid, if you believed the old Nightland sermons. A furnace, if you believed Vael. A child, if you were tired and made mistakes. She did not make that mistake.

"The seventh is inside the city," she said, for the vault, for Halvern, for the dish that would drink him. "We will not chase him through alleys. We will let him come down. He has a habit of running toward dying things." She looked at Sera's small lid and then away from it, which was as close as she came to flinching. "When he does, we chain the six. We snuff him. We keep the dusk we have." Kest swallowed and asked about the frost-queen at the gates, and Solenne told him the truth because the vault was a poor place for comfort. "Then we have two problems, and I have always preferred two problems to a noon."

She turned from the ring and started up the spiral, because the Warm Cell would need a second brazier tonight and the court would need a lie about relics, and because standing over Halvern any longer would turn into a conversation she could not afford. At the third turn she paused and spoke down into the stored heat without looking back. "Stay asleep. All of you. I am still doing this for you." The sixth coffin's note followed her up the stairs like a child at a market stall. She shut it out with the latch, which stuck, as it always stuck. In the Warm Cell the brazier burned at the temperature of a sleeping man, and the black disk of the Hollow Sun, glimpsed through the slit window, hung over Cindrel as it had hung for a thousand years: lightless, watching, and, she was almost certain, no longer entirely asleep.

chapters.title: Orin's Letter
paragraphs: Ren went through the grate shoulder-first and came down in water that had no right to be this cold inside a capital. Cinder landed after him on three legs and shook once, insulted, then put his nose into the dark as if the dark owed him rent. Lyra dropped last, sabers already clear of the coat, the frost-flower crown making a small dry sound against the inner lining like someone tapping a warning. The cistern tunnel ran north under Cindrel in brick the color of old tea. Somewhere above them the Church was counting heat. Somewhere ahead, if Orin's last scrap of chalk had not been a joke, a boy who had publicly sold them was waiting with a lamp he was not supposed to have.

"If he brought a squad, I get the first punch," Lyra said. Ren told her that if Orin had brought a squad, Cinder got the first punch and she could have the second, because he was a generous god. "You are a wet god," she said, and went past him because she still walked like an inquisitor when the ceiling was low.

They moved. Ren kept the Primordial Calor down in the floor of himself the way you kept a coal in a closed fist: present, expensive, stupid to open. Every time he used it the black disk over the world took a slightly more interested breath. He had learned that at the pass, in thirty heartbeats of noon, and he had not stopped learning it since. The cisterns helped. Stone drank leaks. He let a thread of heat-sense run along the mortar, a trick he had copied off a well-guarded in Thornveil and then made quieter, and the thread found a second warmth that was not Lyra and not the dog. Glassheart warmth. Orin's. It sat in a side chamber like a man trying not to be a beacon and failing because he had never been built for dim.

Orin Hale was nineteen and looked like he had not slept in a currency the court accepted. He had a Church coat on, too fine for the cistern, and a bruise along his jaw that had nothing to do with training. When Cinder went to him, tail doing the whole traitorous dance, Orin went down on one knee in the water and put his face in the dog's neck as if that were a legal way to say sorry. Ren stood there with his hands empty and his mouth full of every joke he had practiced and none of them fit. He had let Orin go on the glass steps of the court. He had watched the perfect lie land. It had hurt then. It hurt now in a different register, like coming into a room and finding the fire still lit.

"You look like a tax," Ren said. Orin laughed once, which was a cracked sound, and stood. He asked whether they had followed the chalk marks or the heat, and Ren said the dog had followed him and he had followed the dog and Lyra had followed the part where this was a terrible idea. "Nice collar. Very betray-your-friends. Gold thread. I would have gone with something in 'please kick me.'" Orin said it was the smallest size they had. His gaze ticked to Lyra and away, then back, because he had never been a coward about the things that could cut him. "Cassian's apartments are two levels up and a hymn east. He isn't wearing the harness. He gave me tea. He asked if the boy from Vireth still had manners."

Lyra said, "And you said." Orin said he had said the boy had worse. He reached inside the coat. Ren's heat-sense flared on instinct and found no blade, only paper and a cold knot of Church iron. "I have two things. You can hit me after the second one."

The first thing was a ring of hymn-keys, black iron, each tooth cut in the shape of a note from the dusk-liturgy. Ren had seen keys like that on inquisitors' belts in Vireth, when the wellgate still thought it owned him. These were heavier. Spire keys. Vault keys. The kind of keys a Solar Saint was not supposed to hand to a fallen Hale who had come back with a story. Orin held them out on his palm as if they might bite him, and Lyra took them without touching his skin.

The second thing was a letter. The paper was academy-cheap, folded small, and it had been opened and closed enough times that the crease was dirty. Ren knew that crease. He had watched Orin keep it when he burned Damar Hale's pardon in front of them at Twin Hearth. Private paper. Father-paper, or the nearest wound. Orin did not offer it to Ren. He offered it to the space between them, which was worse. "I copied the vault seals onto the back," Orin said. "Solenne's been inlaying a dish under the six. Reverse pull. If she chains them, it won't shine. It will drink. She built a mouth for you, Ren. I was going to bring this and the keys and go back up before you arrived, which would have been cleaner." He looked at the water around his boots. "I didn't go back up."

That was the stay. It sat in the cistern with them, plain as a third person. Orin could come down into the dark and be their genius again, Glassheart and guilt and the sister-shaped hole, and stop wearing a Church coat that did not fit. Ren felt the old, stupid wanting rise in him, the slum wanting, the wanting that had shared a shard-crumb with a three-legged dog because keeping it would have made him a noble in miniature. He could say *stay* and mean it. He had a history of meaning it at the wrong hours.

Lyra punched Orin once. She did not telegraph it. She had been an inquisitor; telegraphing was for people who wanted applause. The blow caught him on the same jaw as the bruise and turned his face, and Cinder barked, offended on every possible side. Orin did not lift a hand. He spat a bead of blood into the water and waited, which was, Ren thought, the first correct thing he had done with his body all month. "That was for the court," Lyra said. Her voice was dry enough to sand a plank. "The stay is not yours to offer. You are still in their house. If you vanish down here, Solenne will snuff the cisterns and call it a hymn. You will take your pretty keys' absence back to Cassian with a story, and you will keep his door from locking on us while we go down." She flexed her fingers once, as if checking they still belonged to her. "I did not walk a child into a coffin so you could get sentimental in a sewer."

Ren wanted to tell her that the punch had been a little hard. He also wanted to tell Orin that the punch had been a little soft. He did neither. He took the letter because someone had to, and because Orin's hand had started to shake in the small way that meant Glassheart was leaking. The back of the page was a map in a handwriting too neat for the situation: six coffins, a dish, a spiral, a cell at the top marked warm. On the front, Damar Hale's private script offered a son's pardon if the son brought home a boy in a cage. Ren folded it so he would not have to keep seeing the word *cage*. "I'll keep this until you're allowed to burn it," he said. "Don't die in a coat that ugly. Cinder would be embarrassed."

Orin nodded, once, like a man accepting a sentence he had written himself. He touched Cinder's ear, then Ren's shoulder, then nothing, and he went back toward the ladder that led to Cassian's hymn-east apartments. He did not say goodbye. Ren had noticed that the people who meant to come back often forgot the word, and he decided, against evidence, that this was one of those times. He looked at Lyra. She was already turning toward the deeper dark, keys in her fist, crown whispering in the coat, and he followed with Cinder at his heel because the vault was down, and down was the only direction left that was not a cage.

Orin climbed with the taste of blood in his mouth and the Church coat hanging wrong where Lyra's knuckles had landed. The almost-stay went with him like a second bruise. He had stood in the water and felt the old shape of the three of them assemble, Ren's stupid jokes and Lyra's sabers and the dog's ridiculous loyalty, and for a span of heartbeats he had been willing to throw the spy's work down the grate and be Hale-the-traitor in truth. It would have been easier than tea with Cassian. Easier than watching a man with a shard sewn into his chest ask, softly, whether Ren still had manners, as if manners were the wound.

Cassian had given him the hymn-keys without a fight. That was the part Orin would not put in any letter. The Solar Saint had been sitting in a room with the harness on a chair like a shed skin, the well-shard under his sternum ticking at a domestic pace, and he had looked at Orin and said, *If I keep these, she will use me to lock him in. I have been used enough.* Then he had poured tea with a hand that trembled only when the cup was full. Orin had taken the keys and hated how simple it was, hated that mercy from a puppet could feel like a door, hated that he would have to go back now and lie to that same man about a cistern that had been empty.

He paused at the landing and pressed his tongue to the cut inside his cheek. Below, through stone, he felt Ren's heat start to move, Lyra's colder presence beside it, Cinder a small animal spark. They were going down. The letter was in Ren's coat. The dish was waiting. Solenne would feel the seventh the way a locked house felt a broken window. Orin put his court face on, the one that had convinced Damar and Cassian and, once, himself, and he walked toward the apartments with a story about lost keys and frost in the pipes. He did not look back at the grate. Looking back was how you stayed.

chapters.title: Frost at the Gates
paragraphs: Mother Ash came over the outer farms on foot because horses died of her, and because a queen who borrowed a mount looked like a person who needed one. The frost-line ran with her like a hem. Behind her the Nightland host filled the black fields: hollow beasts with lantern ribs, wolves that bowed when she glanced their way, men and women of packed rime who had once been travelers and had asked, in the old manner, to be kept. Cindrel's north gate rose ahead, a mouth of basalt and well-iron, and the Church had already lit the wall-braziers. Stored heat. Tithe heat. Other people's winters stacked into a weapon and pointed at her face.

She did not smile. Smiling was a sun habit. She tasted the city instead, the way she always tasted cities, on the backs of her teeth. Emberwell at the center, fat and mean. Spire above it, singing scarcity. Cisterns under it, wet. And in the cisterns, moving down, a hearth she had already named. Little hearth. Ren Kael, who had sworn to her that he would not restore a sun that belonged to anyone, and who had then gone and become interesting enough that the Church wanted him bottled and the court wanted him crowned and she wanted him seated, simply, in a hall of ice where the cold would finally have a place to put its hands.

The first volley came off the walls as spears of calorancy, gold at the tips, Church-white at the cores. She lifted two fingers. The spears hit a pane of still air and went out with the sound of wet wicks. Her front rank did not break. A hollow stag lowered its antlers, which were not antlers so much as the memory of branching, and scraped a groove in the frozen road as if marking a claim. Mother Ash walked in that groove up to the range where human arrows mattered and stopped, because she had not come to erase a capital. She had come to collect a child before the capital taught him to be a furnace.

Three heats opposed her, and she counted them the way a miser counted coins. The Church on the walls: Solenne's dusk, measured, cruel, competent. The court in its inner rings: a retired saint and a Hale boy telling lies with his shoulders, small warmths trying not to be seen. And the ash-quarters, the uncounted third, where commoners had taken the lesser wellgates and were holding them with pots and bodies and a singing that carried even to her, thin as wire. A three-way siege, then, though only one of the three understood it was a siege. The Church thought it was a defense. The poor thought it was a riot. Mother Ash knew a triangulation when she stood in one. She could have cracked the gate in a dozen breaths. She did not. Cracking the gate would pour her host into streets full of children, and she had not spent a thousand years learning the names of the frozen just to add a city's worth in an afternoon.

"Hold the farms," she said, and the rime-people held. "Eat the tithe-fires on the wall if they throw them. Do not eat the houses." A wolf looked at her with a question in its empty sockets. "The hearth is already inside. We are the door he can still choose. Doors do not stamp."

She put her palm on the north gate's iron. Frost climbed the rivets in ferns. Inside the metal she felt Church seals waking, Solenne's work, old and new, and under those a deeper machinery, a dish, a drinking. The woman in the Spire was preparing to snuff the boy rather than let him be claimed. Mother Ash's mouth went thin. She had offered Ren sanctuary. He had refused a crown of ice with the same stubbornness he refused a crown of gold. That was why she liked him. It was also why she was here, inconveniently, as an army. If he would not sit in her hall she would at least keep the Church from turning him into a cautionary wick.

On the wall a novice shouted a hymn that was supposed to drive frost-spirits back a hundred years. Mother Ash listened to the end out of courtesy. Then she breathed out, and the hymn's heat became a white dust and fell on the archers' sleeves, and the archers learned, in a practical way, that liturgy was not weather.

Nima had lost her left glove in the crowd two streets back and had not gone after it because going after things in a Cindrel riot was how you lost the other glove, and Toma, and the crate they were standing on. The crate belonged to a tallow-seller who had fled when the north gate bells started. From the top of it Nima could see the lesser wellgate of the ash-quarters, the one the Church had shut at dawn, and the people pressed against it with pans and shoulders and a length of chain that had once been a well-guard's. Toma stood at her hip with his chin up, which was how he stood when he was frightened and refusing to give the fright a chair.

"Again," he said. They sang the Vireth well-song because it was the only song they had that was longer than a street and older than a panic. It was not holy. It was what you sang when the shard-crumbs ran out and you needed the little ones to keep their hands moving. Nima's voice was thin. Toma's was all scrape. Together they made a rope. Around the crate, people began to take it up, first the women who had come from Vireth in the same slow leak of refugees that had carried Nima and Toma after Ren's noon, then strangers with Cindrel accents, then a boy with a burned mouth who did not know the words and hummed the shape. Heat did not come from the singing. Nima was not a fool. Heat came from bodies packed together and from the last honest braziers in the quarter and from the fact that if you gave a crowd a meter it stopped crushing itself long enough to be a crowd. Still. The air immediately around the crate stopped biting quite so hard, and Cinder would have liked that, and thinking about Cinder made her throat close, so she sang through it.

A woman in a Church-gray cloak tried to push through to the wellgate with a tithe-seal on a pole. The crowd did not part. Toma, who had once stolen a loaf by looking like a person who had paid, looked like a person who had not paid, and the woman saw the crate and the song and the chain and chose a different street. Nima watched her go and did not feel brave. She felt seventeen streets from home and two friends short. Ren had gone into the capital the way he had gone into every stupid bright thing, and Lyra with him, and the dog, and Nima had followed as far as a girl without Primordial Calor could follow, which turned out to be a crate.

"North gate," Toma said, between verses. He pointed with his chin. Over the roofs the sky had gone the color of a licked tin cup. Frost was climbing the outer walls in sheets. Something with too many joints moved along the battlements and did not fall when the Church threw gold at it. "That's her. The queen. The one from the stories with the wolves."

"She's here for him," Nima said. She did not say Ren's name in a crowd that might sell a name for a coal. "Everybody's here for him. That's the problem with being a boy who lights the sky. You collect armies like fleas."

Toma snorted, which was his laugh when he could not afford a full one, and they picked the song up at the chorus because the little ones at the edge of the crush had started to cry and crying wasted heat. Nima kept her ungloved hand in her armpit and thought, very clearly, that if Ren were here he would have given her his gloves and made a joke about it and then done something ruinous and kind. He was not here. He was under the city, if the rumors about cisterns were worth anything. She sang anyway, because singing was what they had, and because a three-legged dog she loved was down there too, and because the alternative was listening to the wall-bells until her bones learned the tune of being hunted.

The singing was on the fourth repeat when the ground changed its mind. Nima felt it first in the crate, a shiver that was not frost and not crowd. The wellgate's shutters sucked inward, just a finger's width, as if a huge throat under Cindrel had inhaled. All over the ash-quarters the last braziers leaned their flames toward the Spire and then down, down, as if noon had been told to kneel. People screamed in a practical way and grabbed their children. Toma grabbed Nima's sleeve. Over the roofs the Hollow Spire showed a seam of gold that did not rise. It drained. It went into the stone like water into a crack.

Nima did not know the word for what Solenne had just done. She knew the feeling from Vireth, from the night the wellgate ruptured and Ren came up gold and terrified. This was the opposite of that night. This was a mouth opening under the city to drink a boy. She hauled Toma closer on the crate, and she put the song back in her mouth because the little ones were still listening, and because if the world was going to be snuffed she would not let it happen in silence. The frost at the gates kept climbing. The Church kept its bells. Under their feet the Vault of Cinders, which Nima had never seen and would not have named, stood open like a held breath that had finally been allowed to speak.
